summary:
Bulgaria is an EU member state with no criminalisation of gender identity or gender expression, no statute governing which public facilities may be used on the basis of gender, and no entry, visa or border screening that turns on a visitor's recorded gender marker. Same-sex relations have been decriminalised since 1968. A foreign passport is examined on ordinary terms, and a mismatch between presentation and a passport's marker raises no separate question at the border.

The legal framework for changing one's own documents is closed, and that closure is the sharpest trans-specific feature of the country's law. An interpretative decision of the Supreme Court of Cassation of 20 February 2023 holds that 'the only meaning of the term sex should be its biological one' and that the legal system rests on 'the binary existence of humankind', effectively barring legal gender change; the Constitutional Court's verdict on the Istanbul Convention condemned the legislation permitting legal gender recognition. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8 in Y.T. v Bulgaria in 2020 over the refusal of legal gender recognition, and ruled in December 2024 that its obligations were unaffected by that year's registry revision, consistent with P.H. v Bulgaria, with Judge Šimáčková dissenting that the revision decision was over-formalistic. In September 2025 Advocate General Richard de la Tour of the Court of Justice of the European Union issued an opinion that EU law precludes legislation of the Bulgarian kind refusing identity documents matching a trans person's presented gender, and the court concurred with the proposed reasoning; a full judgment remained pending.

Official hostility is written into statute. On 7 August 2024 Bulgaria's parliament passed an amendment to the education law banning 'propaganda, promotion, or incitement... directly or indirectly' of ideas about 'non-traditional sexual orientation and/or gender identity other than the biological one' in the education system; it was introduced by the Revival party, backed by GERB, signed by President Rumen Radev and entered into force on 16 August 2024. A visitor accompanying family or attending a course may encounter this restriction, which has no exception for foreign nationals.

Protection on the books is undercut by non-enforcement. Anti-discrimination legislation in force since 2004 prohibits direct and indirect discrimination in housing, education and medical treatment and has banned hate speech on the ground of sexual orientation since 1 January 2004; a 2015 amendment extended coverage to 'sex' as including 'sex change', although gender expression and gender identity are not named explicitly. Amnesty International's February 2015 review found that authorities consistently fail to identify and adequately investigate hate crimes, with bias attacks spiking in 2013 per the Bulgarian Helsinki Committee left unpursued though the Sofia Prosecution opened some cases. A January 2014 government commitment to outlaw hate crimes against LGBT people was dropped by the government formed after the October 2014 elections; heavier penalties for sexual-orientation-based crimes were adopted on 28 July 2023. Reported cases that went unaddressed include the 2008 killing of a 25-year-old student in a Sofia park by a group intending to 'cleanse' the park of gay people, and the assault of children as young as 14 or 15 in Plovdiv on 27 September 2020 by ultra-fans of Botev in an anti-LGBT 'cleansing action'.

Public visibility carries a documented violence risk that is managed by police presence rather than removed. The first Sofia Pride in 2008, with about 150 participants, was attacked with petrol bombs, rocks and glass bottles and more than 60 hooligans were arrested; far-right extremists marred the 2008 and 2010 editions, and the fourth annual parade in June 2011 passed without incident under heavy police guard while a 'Family NGO' protested. In the run-up to the 10 June 2017 march, Human Rights Watch recorded a group called the National Resistance rallying counter-demonstrators to 'cleanse Sofia from garbage'. In November 2009 the District Council of Pazardzhik voted to forbid the 'public demonstration of sexual or any other orientation'; the Administrative Court struck it down in October 2010 for procedural errors and then upheld it on appeal in July 2011.

Entry and residence questions for a visitor travelling with a partner turn on relationship law rather than gender law. Article 46 of the Constitution has defined marriage as a union between a man and a woman since 1991, and no civil unions exist. A Sofia court on 29 June 2018 granted an Australian woman and her French wife, married in France in 2016, the right to live in Bulgaria under the Coman ruling, after residency had been denied a year earlier; a couple who married in the UK had their recognition claim rejected by the Sofia Administrative Court in January 2018, an appeal pursued by Deystvie. In September 2023 the European Court of Human Rights held that Bulgaria's refusal to recognise same-sex couples is an 'infringement of human rights', a case still subject to appeal and awaiting a government response.
tangentialFactors:
Official and institutional rhetoric supplies context for the statutory position. The Bulgarian Orthodox Church calls pride events a 'sinful demonstration'; billboards promoting tolerance toward same-sex couples in Varna and Burgas were vandalised in December 2018; the far-right National Resistance has advocated brooms and shovels against pride attendees and the Ataka party has held protests against LGBT events. The period 2020 to 2021 saw a documented rise in anti-LGBT rhetoric in which 'gender became a slur'. The 1964 show trial of 26 men, including actor Georgi Partsalev and singer Emil Dimitrov, was described by experts as 'a masquerade for the public' about 'decadent Western culture', and is the historical marker of state-directed hostility.

Comparative placement is weak: ILGA-Europe ranked Bulgaria 37 of 49 European countries for LGBT rights protection in 2020. Local hostility has reached formal prohibition twice, in the Pazardzhik council vote of November 2009 and in the national education amendment of August 2024, and the two follow a similar pattern of restriction justified on moral grounds.

Age of consent has been 14 regardless of sex since 2002 and is 16 as of 2026. A 2008 survey of 15 schools in Sofia, Varna and Plovdiv found 10.5% of students identified as bisexual and 1.8% as gay, with 29% saying they would refuse to sit next to a gay classmate, 5% saying they would bully gay classmates and 39% saying they would protect them.
localsOnly:
Residents cannot obtain legal gender recognition: the Supreme Court of Cassation's interpretative decision of 20 February 2023 fixes sex as biological and the legal system as binary, and the Constitutional Court's Istanbul Convention verdict condemned the enabling legislation. The 2020 Y.T. v Bulgaria judgment and the December 2024 ruling establish the contrary obligation without reopening the registry.

Same-sex couples hold no recognised partnership. Article 46 of the Constitution bans same-sex marriage, no civil union exists, and the denial extends to inheritance, joint property and medical decision-making: same-sex partners cannot make medical decisions for each other. Same-sex couples are banned from adopting. A Bulgarian court recognised a same-sex marriage performed in France in 2019. In September 2023 the European Court of Human Rights found non-recognition an 'infringement of human rights', with appeal pending. A 2021 Court of Justice of the European Union ruling forced Bulgaria to issue an ID to a child of a lesbian couple after it refused a birth certificate.

Health services are covered by the anti-discrimination ban on sexual-orientation discrimination in force since 1 January 2004, and housing, education and medical treatment are protected against direct and indirect discrimination under the 2004 act as expanded in 2015 to 'sex change'. Gay and bisexual men are not explicitly barred from donating blood: the donor form, under a Ministry of Healthcare ordinance of 19 July 2004, does not ask orientation but requires confirmation of no HIV or STI-risk practices.

Intersex newborns routinely have male genitalia removed as the 'the easier operation', with parents 'rarely informed' of later harm to the child's gender identity, and there are no laws concerning intersex people. Support infrastructure exists at community level: the Single Step Foundation, founded 2016, works with LGBTI youth on coming out and affirmation, and launched Bulgaria's first licensed online support chat in October 2017 for LGBTI youth, families and allies.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Court of Justice of the European Union has issued a full judgment on the September 2025 Advocate General opinion, or whether Bulgaria has since opened a route to legal gender recognition, is unresolved in this record; the sources describe the opinion and the court's agreement with the Advocate General's reasoning while the judgment was pending.

The status of the September 2023 European Court of Human Rights case on same-sex couple recognition is unresolved beyond 'subject to appeals and awaiting a government response'. Whether the heavier penalties for sexual-orientation-based crimes adopted on 28 July 2023 have changed the pattern of non-investigation documented by Amnesty International in February 2015 is not sourced here.

It is not sourced whether the August 2024 education amendment has been applied against foreign students or visitors, or how the Pazardzhik demonstration prohibition of July 2011 has been enforced since. Claims drawn from the Wikipedia-derived inventory rest on that source's own citations and were not independently verified for this record.
